newsitem.title: JAPAN: Matsushita profits boosted by high-tech goods, yen.
newsitem.headline: Matsushita profits boosted by high-tech goods, yen.

text.p: Japanese consumer electronics giant Matsushita Electric Industrial Co unveiled a healthy rise in annual profits on Thursday, bolstered by robust sales of high-technology products and the weak yen.

Clearly on the road to recovery from a consumer electronics slump in the early 1990s, Matsushita, which sells under the National and Panasonic brands, said the benefits of the weak yen, cost-cutting and robust sales more than offset a slump in prices for its products.

"In the (1996/97) business year, production and sales units at home and abroad performed steadily and group sales reached their highest ever," director Susumu Ishihara told a news conference in Tokyo.

Matsushita posted a group net profit of 137.85 billion yen ($1.18 billion) in the year which ended in March, exceeding its latest forecast of 120 billion yen ($1.03 billion) and scoring a substantial improvement over its loss of 56.87 billion yen ($490 million) in the previous year.
Net profit is equal to current profit, which is pre-tax, minus taxes and extraordinary profits and losses.

The loss two years ago reflected the 1995 sale of U.S. film maker MCA Inc, now named Universal Studios Inc, but even excluding the impact of the money-losing sale, Matsushita's net profits in 1996/97 grew by 28 percent, the company said.
For the current year, the company said group net profit would grow about 10 percent to 152 billion yen ($1.31 billion).

Matsushita's parent current profit managed an even more impressive gain of nearly 40 percent to 143.31 billion yen ($1.23 billion) last business year, with further growth to 155 billion yen ($1.33 billion) predicted for this year.

Analysts said the firm's strategy of shifting towards high-tech goods from traditional consumer electronics had begun to bear fruit, as it looks set for strong sales of cellular phones, batteries and various computer-related goods.
Group net sales grew 13 percent to hit a record 7.68 trillion yen ($66.2 billion) in 1996/97, helped by a solid 24 percent rise in sales of communications and industrial equipment.
The company said it will maintain its drive towards high-tech goods.

A Matsushita spokesman said before the earnings announcement that the company would maintain its level of capital investment in the semiconductor sector at about 100 billion yen ($862 million) in 1997/98, while increasing spending on liquid crystal displays (LCDs) for computer screens.
In total, the firm said its group capital spending would rise by 13 percent to 470 billion yen ($4.05 billion) this fiscal year.

Analysts said Matsushita would probably outperform most of its competitors in sales of audiovisual goods and household appliances, despite intensifying price competition in these sectors and the prospect of a shrinking domestic market.

Along with other exporters such as Sony Corp, Matsushita is a major beneficiary of the weak yen, which makes goods more price-competitive overseas. The dollar averaged around 113 yen in 1996/97 versus 97 yen the year before.
Ishihara said the weak yen boosted the firm's group profit by 150 billion yen ($1.29 billion) in 1996/97.

He said the company assumed a dollar/yen rate of 115 yen in making its latest earnings estimates for 1997/98. The dollar edged up to about 116 yen on Thursday after slumping earlier in the week below 112 yen to its lowest level since December.

In an attempt to trim the risks from unpredictable currency swings, Matsushita plans to exchange foreign currencies earned from exports with group companies that need to make non-yen payments. By doing so, the company could also save on exchange commissions it pays to banks.
The move is in line with a planned revision of Japanese law to allow companies to exchange foreign currencies without going through banks, the spokesman said. ($1=116 yen)
